involve.intro: Amplify is open source: its code, content and checks are public on GitHub, and anyone can help build, check and look after it. You do not need to code. Pick what fits your time.

rules: Everything on GitHub is public. Never post your name, school, address, phone, email or photo, or anyone else's.
GitHub accounts are for people aged 13 and over. If you are 13 to 17, agree it with a parent or carer first. Under 13s can take part through a trusted adult.
Be kind and constructive. Disagree with ideas, not people.
If you are worried about yourself or someone else, do not post on GitHub. Go to Safeguarding & support.
A person reviews every change before it goes live, and the automated checks must pass. Nothing is published automatically.

how.d: README.md explains the project, and CONTRIBUTING.md explains how to help.
Choose an issue, or open one describing what you want to do.
Edit data files in data/ for content, or the tools/ scripts for features. Never edit site/ by hand: it is built.
Run the checks. Each one also proves it still catches a deliberate mistake.
Open a pull request. The owner reviews and decides what is merged and published.

ambassadors.status: Pilot: the programme opens when the portal owner confirms it can be run safely (open item O12). Until then you can register interest.
ambassadors.intro: Ambassadors and champions help young people, families and professionals find Amplify, use it well and tell us what they need. There are three levels; start wherever suits you.

tiers.who: Anyone, any age (under 13s with a trusted adult).
does: Shares the portal with friends, family, a class or a group
Tells us what is useful or missing
Takes part in UK Parliament Week

tiers.who: Young people 13 and over, parents, teachers, youth workers and club leaders.
does: Runs at least one session from Training each term
Collects feedback from the group (no personal details)
Checks one theme's sources each quarter

tiers.who: 16 and over; 13 to 15 with a named adult who agrees to support them.
does: Represents Amplify at events such as UK Parliament Week
Helps plan what the portal does next

promise: Your safety comes first. Ambassadors under 18 always have a named adult contact, and are never asked to meet anyone alone.
No one is asked for personal details on GitHub. Registration asks only for your role, nation, age band and what you would like to do.
Recognition: a digital badge, a credit in the release log (first name or a nickname only, if you want one), and a reference for your volunteering on request.
You can stop at any time, without giving a reason.
conduct: Describe Amplify accurately: it is independent and unofficial, not a UK Youth Parliament, National Youth Agency or UK Parliament service.
Never share a young person's name, image or story without their agreement and, if they are under 18, a parent's or carer's consent.
Follow your school's, club's or employer's safeguarding policy whenever you run a session.
Point people to the helplines on Safeguarding & support, never to your own contact details.

posts.text: Amplify is a new, independent and open-source portal that helps young people across the UK be heard: trusted sources, safeguarding, campaign tools and a route into youth voice for every age. It launches in UK Parliament Week, 23 to 29 November 2026. Anyone can help build it, no coding needed.

Want to know how to make your voice heard? Amplify brings together trusted sources, guides and safe ways to take part in youth voice across England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland. Ask your teacher or youth worker for the link during UK Parliament Week.

During UK Parliament Week we will be using Amplify, a free portal about youth voice and democracy. It does not ask young people to sign in or share personal details. A Parents and carers tour explains how you can support your child to take part safely.

Our club is helping build a real open-source portal for young people. We will learn how professional teams check, test and release software, and every change we make is reviewed before it goes live. Girls and young women especially welcome: you belong in tech.

campaign.social_note: Social media and messaging apps have their own minimum ages (usually 13), and the government plans further restrictions for under 16s. Posts are for adults and allies to share; young people can share with a parent's or carer's agreement where the platform allows.
campaign.hashtag_note: #UKParliamentWeek is the event's own hashtag (a lead to confirm with UK Parliament Education before use). #AmplifyYouthVoice is this portal's own.

assembly.title: A five-minute assembly: Your voice, carried further
steps: Ask: hands up who has an opinion about something in school, in your area or in the news. (Everyone.)
Say: in a democracy, opinions only change things when they reach the people who decide. That is what youth voice is.
Show three real routes: the Make Your Mark ballot, your Member of Youth Parliament, and your local youth council.
Explain UK Parliament Week: events across the UK about how Parliament works and how to be heard.
Invite: find Amplify, try Your route in, and tell a teacher one issue you would raise.

stem.intro: A special shout-out to young people in science, technology, engineering and maths, and especially to girls and young women who code, build, design and engineer, or who might. Tech decides a lot about young people's lives; it should be built by people like them.

facts.f: Women were 27.2% of the UK's core STEM workforce in September 2025, and over 1.4 million women work in core STEM roles.
Women are 16.9% of the UK's engineering and technology workforce.
Girls' A-level computing entries rose by 149% between 2019 and 2025.
Over 96,000 girls have taken part in the CyberFirst Girls Competition since it began; from 1 September 2026 CyberFirst became part of TechFirst.
facts.src: NCSC CyberFirst annual report 2025-26 and NCSC

facts.f: There are over 2,000 free Code Clubs meeting in UK schools and libraries.

paths.first: Join a free Code Club or CoderDojo. You do not need to know anything to start.
Ask your school about TechYouth activities and the TechFirst Girls Competition.
Enter The Big Bang Competition with a project you care about.
16 to 18 in London? Watch for the next Open City Accelerate round.

paths.p: For girls, young women and non-binary young people

devops.intro: DevOps means building, testing, releasing and running software as one team, with automation doing the repetitive checking. This portal is a small but real example, so you can learn on it.

steps.d: Every change is a commit on GitHub, so nothing is lost and everything can be undone.
The published page is generated from data files by a build script, never edited by hand.
Dozens of checks look for broken links, missing safeguards, stale helplines and accessibility problems.
Each check is run against a deliberately broken copy to prove it would catch the problem.
steps.where: The 'caught' lines in every check's output

steps.d: GitHub Actions runs every check, in a real browser too, on every proposed change.
A weekly health run re-checks everything and reports to one issue.
Automation never publishes. A person reviews, merges and releases.

stem.note: Listing an organisation is not an endorsement. Check each one's age rules and safeguarding before you sign up, and ask a parent or carer if you are under 16.
